english: Hello, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team
usage: Hello, this is Kim Minsu from the Marketing team
The standard opening line of almost every work email
Hello, this is ○○○, the person in charge of ○○
When the reader may not know you; states your role
This is Assistant Manager ○○○ from ○○ Company
To an external party; lead with company + title
Good day, this is ○○○ from the ○○ team
More formal 하십니까 for very senior or official mail
examples: 안녕하세요, 김민수입니다.
Hello, this is Kim Minsu.
The minimum: greeting plus your name and -입니다
안녕하세요, 영업팀 김민수입니다. 어제 통화드린 건으로 메일 드립니다.
Hello, this is Kim Minsu from Sales. I'm writing about the matter we discussed by phone yesterday.
Greeting, then immediately state WHY you're writing
안녕하세요, ABC회사 영업팀 김민수 대리입니다. 다름이 아니라 견적 관련해서 연락드렸습니다.
Hello, this is Assistant Manager Kim Minsu from ABC Company's Sales team. I'm contacting you regarding the quote.
External, formal: company + team + name + title + reason
nuance: Korean work emails almost always open with 안녕하세요 + your identity in the pattern [team/company] + [name] + [optional title] + 입니다. This is not optional fluff; jumping straight into the request feels abrupt and rude in Korean office culture. The verb 입니다 here means 'I am ~', and you state your OWN name plainly, never with honorific 님 attached to yourself (writing 김민수님입니다 about yourself is wrong — 님 honors others, not you). Note the title order differs from English: Koreans say 김민수 대리 (name THEN rank), not 대리 김민수. The nearest variant is 안녕하십니까, which is one notch more formal/official (used in announcements, to very senior people, or in 합쇼체 letters); everyday inter-office mail uses 안녕하세요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is translating 'My name is' as 제 이름은 ~예요, which sounds like a self-introduction in a textbook, not a professional email; the natural business form is simply [name]입니다. Also avoid 저는 ~입니다 with 저는 every time — Korean drops the 'I' once context is clear, so 김민수입니다 alone is cleaner than 저는 김민수입니다.

english: Please take note / for your reference
usage: Polite-formal; asks the reader to keep it in mind
Just for your reference (no action needed)
Signals it's FYI only, nothing to do
Curt note-style ending, internal memos/superiors to juniors
examples: 아래 내용 참고 부탁드립니다.
Please take note of the content below.
Points the reader to information you've included
회의 전에 첨부 자료 참고 부탁드립니다.
Please review the attached materials before the meeting.
Combines 참고 with a deadline ('before the meeting')
지난번과 일정이 변경되었으니 참고 부탁드립니다.
The schedule has changed from last time, so please take note.
Used to flag a change the reader should be aware of

It's a soft, information-sharing closer: you're not demanding an action, just asking the reader to be AWARE of something. The feeling is courteous and low-pressure. The crucial contrast is with 참조 (參照): in email, 참조 is the CC field ('참조: 박과장님') — it names who's copied — whereas 참고 means 'for your information/reference'. English speakers constantly confuse these because both translate loosely as 'reference'; if you write 참조 부탁드립니다 meaning 'please note this', it reads oddly like 'please CC this'. Another contrast: 참고하세요 (plain imperative 'refer to it') is fine to juniors/peers but can sound slightly directive to a superior; 참고 부탁드립니다 with 부탁드리다 is humbler and safer upward. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'FYI' as needing a verb of command; in Korean the humble-request frame 부탁드립니다 carries the politeness, so don't stack it with a blunt 하세요. Note 참고 is a 하다-noun, so to make it a verb you need 참고하다 — never 참고 주세요 (you can't 'give' a reference).

usage: Polite-formal; states the file is attached
Adds 드리다 to sound a touch more courteous
Pairs the attachment with a request to open it
Crisp present-tense form, common in quick mail

I've attached the materials you requested.

견적서 첨부해 드리니 확인 부탁드립니다.
I'm attaching the quote, so please review it.

수정된 보고서를 다시 첨부드립니다. 이전 파일은 삭제해 주세요.

Real situation: resending a corrected version

A frequent English-speaker pitfall is over-literal 'please find attached' rendered as 첨부된 것을 찾아 주세요 ('please go look for the attached thing'), which sounds like the file is lost; you simply state 첨부했습니다. usage: The default polite-formal request to review something
Softer, slightly less stiff than 드립니다
Adds an explicit reply step after checking
examples: 내용 확인 부탁드립니다.
Please check the content.
Asks the reader to review what you wrote/sent

Please confirm whether the schedule works for you.

Please confirm the amounts below are correct; let me know if there's any issue.
Real: asks to verify figures and invites a flag

usage: Polite-formal; asks for a written response
답장 is the everyday word for a reply/letter back
I'd be grateful for your reply
Attaches a deadline to the reply request
examples: 검토 후 회신 부탁드립니다.
Please reply after reviewing.
Asks them to review, then respond
바쁘시겠지만 금요일까지 회신 부탁드립니다.
I know you're busy, but please reply by Friday.
바쁘시겠지만 softens a deadline request
혹시 참석 가능하신지 회신 주시면 일정 잡겠습니다.

Real: reply ties directly to a next action

The contrast to watch: 회신 (a reply, the act of writing back) vs. 답변 (答辯, the ANSWER itself to a specific question). If you posed a concrete question and want that answer, 답변 부탁드립니다 fits; for a general 'please get back to me', use 회신. 지난주에 보내드린 견적 관련해서 확인 부탁드린 건 어떻게 되었을까요? 일정이 있어 여쭤봅니다.

english: If you review and share feedback, I'll incorporate it
usage: I'll incorporate your feedback after you review
Polite; invites comments and promises to apply them

nuance: 참조에 넣어 주세요 is 참조 ('reference/CC', Sino-Korean 參照) + 에 ('into') + 넣다 ('to put in') + 주세요 ('please'). In Korean email, 참조 (參照) is literally the CC field, and 참조에 넣다 ('put into CC') means to copy someone — the everyday office phrase for keeping a colleague in the loop. This is the critical contrast that trips English speakers: 참조 (參照, the CC line) vs. 참고 (參考, 'for your reference/FYI'). They look and sound nearly identical and both gloss as 'reference' in English, but 참조 = the CC recipients, while 참고 = 'please take note'. Saying 참고에 넣어 주세요 is wrong — you don't 'put someone into FYI'. The other field words: 받는 사람 (To), 참조 (CC), 숨은 참조 (BCC). The English-speaker pitfall is using the loanword and writing 씨씨에 넣어 주세요 (CC as 씨씨) — understood in casual chat but not standard business Korean; use 참조. Another trap: the verb is 넣다 ('put in') with the particle 에 (참조'에' 넣다), not 참조를 넣다 in the sense of inserting a thing — you put the PERSON into the 참조 field. To say you copied someone, it's 참조로 넣었습니다 or 참조에 넣었습니다.
